Doctor: mm-hmm
Patient: and i fell and i think i twisted my knee in some kind of funky way
Doctor: okay that that that that's not good how old are your niece

Patient: yeah
Doctor: that sounds fun but i'm i'm sad as you hurt your knee doing it so for your knee pain are you are you able to bear weight on that leg the left leg
Patient: well i've been limping ever since and it really has n't gotten better so i thought it was maybe time to come see you because it happened about a week ago

Patient: honestly it's been hurting on both sides more so on the inside than the the outside
Doctor: so okay so more in the medial aspect less on the lateral okay that makes sense and you said did you hear a pop when you when you twisted it

Doctor: okay alright so how would you rate your pain with your knee out of out of one to ten

Doctor: alright any other questions
Patient: no that's it
Doctor: alright great thanks

Left knee pain, possible medial collateral ligament (MCL) strain.

1. Prescribe tramadol 50 mg twice daily for pain.

5. Recommend avoiding running for the next three weeks to allow healing.

Patient: sure .
Doctor: and kick against my hands .
Doctor: okay , good . all right .
Doctor: okay , so ... on physical examination , you know , i-i do hear a slight 2 out of 6 s- s- systolic heart murmur .
Patient: mm-hmm .
Doctor: on your heart exam . which you've had in the past .
Patient: mm-hmm .
Doctor: so that sounds stable to me .
Doctor: on your back exam , you know , you do have some pain to palpation of the lumbar spine . and you have pain with flexion and extension of the back . and you have a negative straight leg raise , which is which is good . so , let's- let's just look at some of your results , okay ?

Patient: mm-hmm .
Doctor: . the history , okay ?
Patient: mm-hmm .
Doctor: so let's just go ahead and we'll- we're going to go over , you know , my assessment and my plan for you .
Doctor: so for your first problem , your back pain . you know , i think you have a lumbar strain from the lifting . so , let's go ahead . we can prescribe you some meloxicam 15 mg once a day .
Patient: mm-hmm .
Doctor: i want you to continue to ice it , okay . i want you to try to avoid any strenuous activity and we can go ahead and- and refer you to physical therapy-
Patient: mm-hmm .
Doctor: . and see how you do , okay ?
Patient: you got it .

On examination, there is pain to palpation of the lumbar spine and pain with flexion and extension. X-ray of the back is normal. The assessment includes lumbar strain, uncontrolled diabetes, and elevated blood pressure. The plan includes prescribing meloxicam, increasing metformin and lisinopril, ordering a hemoglobin A1c test, and referring to physical therapy.

reference:
SUBJECTIVE:
The patient is a 58-year-old male with a past medical history significant for diabetes type 2, hypertension, and osteoarthritis, who presents today with back pain. He reports that he was helping his daughter move heavy equipment and lifted some heavy boxes too quickly on Saturday. He thought he heard a pop when he moved and had to lie down for about an hour before the pain resolved. He has had stiffness ever since. The pain is located in his lower back. He took Tylenol, ibuprofen, and used Icy Hot on the area, but it did not seem to help. He endorsed some tingling in his toes on his right foot, which resolved on Sunday afternoon. He finds it difficult to find a comfortable position to sleep at night and tends to lie on his right side, which helps a little. Regarding his diabetes, he reports that he has not had a home-cooked meal in weeks due to travel and admits to dietary indiscretions. He monitors his blood pressure at home and reports it is under control for the most part. Regarding his osteoarthritis, he reports occasional aggravation of his knee when he runs too much or lifts boxes that are too heavy. The patient denies chest pain, nausea, vomiting, fevers, and chills.

OBJECTIVE:
Cardiovascular: Slight 2/6 systolic ejection murmur. Musculoskeletal: Pain to palpation of the lumbar spine. Pain with flexion and extension of the back. Negative straight leg raise. Vitals: Blood pressure is elevated. Results: Hemoglobin A1c is elevated at 8. X-ray of the back is unremarkable with normal bony alignment and no fracture present.

ASSESSMENT:
Lumbar strain. Diabetes type 2. Hypertension. Osteoarthritis.

PLAN:
1. Initiate meloxicam 15 mg once a day.
2. Encourage continued icing of the affected area and avoidance of strenuous activity.
3. Refer to physical therapy.
4. Increase metformin to 1000 mg twice a day.
5. Repeat hemoglobin A1c in 6 months.
6. Increase lisinopril from 10 mg to 20 mg a day.
7. Continue to monitor knee for osteoarthritis; no further workup is needed at this time.

Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: Hi there! I am Doctor [NAME], sir.
Patient: Hello! It is nice to meet you.
Doctor: What brings you into see me today?
Patient: I have had this weakness in my right leg for quite some time now.
Doctor: How long has this been going on and do you know how you injured yourself?
Patient: I think that it was about six months ago that the weakness in my leg started. I don't really remember how it happened.
Doctor: Can you tell me what you do remember?
Patient: I was reaching to get something from a cabinet, and I noticed that I was unable to stand on my right toe. Ever since then I have had difficulty pushing off when walking. My toes were tingling and numb.
Doctor: Was the numbness and tingling mild, moderate, or severe?
Patient: It was a mild feeling, but this has been an ongoing problem that has been the same since the weakness started.
Doctor: Have you had any other pain any where else in your body?
Patient: I have had back pain, but this has been going on for many years and has not changed.
Doctor: Is the back pain been mild, moderate, or severe?
Patient: I would say mild. I have also been having cramping in both calves.
Doctor: How long has that been going on?
Patient: For the past year but it stopped about two months ago.
Doctor: Have you had any weakness in the left leg?
Patient: No. I don't think so.
Doctor: Have you had any pain around right leg and the area of numbness and tingling?
Patient: No. Everything that is going on with my right leg has pretty much been the same since it started six months ago. I have not gotten worse or better.
Doctor: Have you had any bowel or bladder incontinence? Any radicular pain?
Patient: No.
Doctor: When did you first see a doctor for the issue? I remember that you told me you saw a different provider prior to coming to see me.
Patient: I saw the other doctor in October. That was a couple of months before I came to see you.
Doctor: I see in your chart that we did a CT scan that shows degenerative changes, but nothing obviously abnormal. Remind me why we did not do a MRI of your spine?
Patient: I cannot have an MRI because of my ear implant.
Doctor: That is unfortunate. It looks like we were able to do an EMG and nerve conduction studies. What medications are you taking currently?
Patient: I had an elevated CK before I started taking stat medications.
Doctor: What medications are those?
Patient: I am not taking Lipitor anymore. I think I took it for about fifteen months.
Doctor: Do you know what your levels of your CK were before you started taking medication?
Patient: I thought that my CK was in the five hundred or six hundreds prior to starting it. Once I started it, my levels increased to about eight hundred and then came down to about five hundred again when it was stopped. I recently stopped taking Lipitor because my levels were up to the thousand's and then my CK apparently has returned to about the five hundreds or six hundreds.
Doctor: I don't see any labs in your chart. Did your primary do labs for your CK levels?
Patient: Yes, he did.
Doctor: Okay. Have you started any other medications?
Patient: Yes, I just started Zetia.
Doctor: Have you experienced any weakness or pain after starting Zetia?
Patient: No.
Doctor: Can you remind me how old you are?
Patient: I am fifty-five.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Emergency department provider dictation. The patient is a 65-year-old male who presented with right lower quadrant abdominal pain that began yesterday evening around the umbilicus and over about twelve hours moved to the right lower quadrant. He describes the pain as sharp and constant, eight out of ten, worse with walking and coughing. He has had nausea and loss of appetite since this morning. He denies vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, blood in the stool, dysuria, hematuria, and testicular pain. He also denies chest pain and shortness of breath. Past medical history is hypertension and type 2 diabetes, and he has had no prior abdominal surgery. Home medications are lisinopril 20 mg daily and metformin 1000 mg twice daily. Allergies, and this is important, he reports an allergy to ibuprofen with hives and facial swelling, and says the same happens with naproxen, so we are avoiding NSAIDs.

Vital signs at triage, blood pressure 152 over 88, heart rate 96, respiratory rate 18, temperature 100.4 degrees Fahrenheit, correction, 100.2 degrees Fahrenheit on recheck, and oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. On exam he is uncomfortable but nontoxic appearing. Heart and lungs are normal. The abdomen is soft with focal tenderness over McBurney's point, voluntary guarding, and rebound tenderness in the right lower quadrant, with no rigidity and no distension. Rovsing sign is positive. Testicular and hernia exams are normal.

ED course. Labs show white blood cell count 14.8 with neutrophil predominance, hemoglobin 14.2, creatinine 1.0, glucose 168, and a normal lactate. Urinalysis shows no blood and no signs of infection. CT of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast shows a dilated appendix measuring 12 millimeters with periappendiceal fat stranding and a small appendicolith, with no abscess, no perforation, and no free air. He received a liter of normal saline, morphine 4 mg IV, acetaminophen 1000 mg IV, ondansetron 4 mg IV, ceftriaxone 2 g IV, and metronidazole 500 mg IV. Pain improved to three out of ten after treatment.

Medical decision making. This is acute uncomplicated appendicitis. Ureteral stone is less likely given the clean urinalysis and CT, and diverticulitis is not seen on imaging. Because he received IV contrast and has diabetes, I am holding the metformin and starting sliding scale insulin while he is in the hospital. Lisinopril will continue at the home dose.

Disposition. General surgery has evaluated the patient and he will be admitted for laparoscopic appendectomy. He is NPO. Continue ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 24 hours and metronidazole 500 mg IV every 8 hours. Continue morphine 4 mg IV as needed for pain. Avoid NSAIDs. Repeat creatinine in the morning.
"""

Impression: Generalized anxiety disorder with a partial response to sertraline 50 mg after six weeks, tolerating the medication well. Caffeine intake is likely contributing to the sleep difficulty and muscle tension.

Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: Thanks for coming in. I understand you are a 52-year-old female with diabetes, high blood pressure, hypothyroidism, and high cholesterol, on IV antibiotics for a bone infection in your foot, and the home infusion nurse sent you because of loose stools and some soreness at the line. Is that right?
Patient: Yes. I have been getting the ceftriaxone through my PICC line for about three weeks, and for two days now I have had loose stools, like four or five a day.
Doctor: Remind me what the infection was.
Patient: Osteomyelitis in the bone behind my big toe, on the left foot. It came from a diabetic foot ulcer that would not heal. They did an MRI and a bone biopsy, and it grew MSSA.
Doctor: Right. And ceftriaxone 2 grams once a day, planned for six weeks?
Patient: Yes, six weeks total.
Doctor: Any fever or chills?
Patient: No fever, no chills. No blood in the stool, and no belly pain, just a little cramping.
Doctor: Any redness, swelling or pus at the PICC site, or swelling of the arm?
Patient: The spot is a little sore, but no pus and my arm is not swollen. No rash either, and no shortness of breath.
Doctor: Good. Let's go through what you take. Please include the over-the-counter things.
Patient: Metformin 1000 milligrams twice a day, lisinopril 10 milligrams in the morning, levothyroxine 75 micrograms, and atorvastatin 20 milligrams at night. For supplements I take magnesium oxide 400 milligrams every day for leg cramps, and vitamin D 5000 units daily. Oh wait, the vitamin D is 2000 units, the 5000 was the old bottle.
Doctor: So vitamin D 2000 units daily. How long have you been taking the magnesium?
Patient: About a month, since I started the antibiotic. I read it helps the bones.
Doctor: Okay. Any allergies to medicines?
Patient: No drug allergies.
Doctor: Your vitals today are blood pressure 128/76, heart rate 88, temperature 98.9 Fahrenheit, and oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air. The PICC site is mildly tender with no redness, no drainage, and no cord along the vein. The belly is soft and non-tender, with normal bowel sounds. The left foot wound is clean, pink, and smaller than at your last visit. Your labs from this morning show a white count of 8.9, creatinine 1.6, which is up from 1.1 two weeks ago, and an eGFR of 38. The ESR is 62, down from 98. The C. diff test on your stool sample is negative.
Patient: Is the bone infection getting better, then?
Doctor: Yes, the wound and the ESR trend both look better. I think the loose stools are mostly from the magnesium on top of the antibiotic and the metformin. The kidney number is also up, and with the eGFR at 38 the metformin dose is too high.
Patient: So what do I change?
Doctor: Here is my impression. First, osteomyelitis of the left foot from a diabetic foot ulcer, improving on IV ceftriaxone. Second, diarrhea, most likely from the magnesium supplement, and the C. diff test is negative. Third, a mild rise in creatinine, so I am reducing the metformin from 1000 milligrams twice daily to 500 milligrams twice daily. Stop the magnesium oxide today. You can keep the vitamin D. Continue the ceftriaxone 2 grams IV daily through the full six weeks, and keep the lisinopril, levothyroxine, and atorvastatin the same. Drink plenty of fluids.
Patient: Should I stop the lisinopril too, because of the kidneys?
Doctor: Good question. I would keep taking it for now. We will repeat the kidney labs in 3 days with the home infusion nurse, along with the weekly CBC, ESR, and CRP. I will also message your infectious disease clinic about today's visit, and you keep your appointment there next week. If you develop fever, bloody diarrhea, severe belly pain, or redness or swelling at the PICC site or arm, go to the emergency department.
Patient: Okay, I understand. Thank you.
"""

She continues methotrexate 15 mg once weekly with folic acid 1 mg daily as prescribed. Over the last six weeks she has had swelling and pain in the right second and third fingers, morning stiffness lasting about 90 minutes, and a sausage-like swelling of the right third finger. Her scaly plaques on the elbows and scalp have also worsened. She is taking naproxen 500 mg twice daily with partial relief and lisinopril 10 mg daily for hypertension. Stop naproxen because of the blood pressure; continue lisinopril 10 mg daily and have primary care recheck her blood pressure in two weeks. Refer to our social worker and pharmacy team to apply for the manufacturer copay assistance program, and restart adalimumab 40 mg every other week once it is approved. Rheumatology outpatient dictation. This is a 57-year-old female with psoriatic arthritis and plaque psoriasis, here for follow-up of a flare. She tells me she has taken her adalimumab 40 mg, which is supposed to be every other week, only about once a month for the past four months because the copay went up and she cannot afford it. She continues methotrexate 15 mg once weekly with folic acid 1 mg daily as prescribed. Over the last six weeks she has had swelling and pain in the right second and third fingers, morning stiffness lasting about 90 minutes, and a sausage-like swelling of the right third finger. Her scaly plaques on the elbows and scalp have also worsened. She is taking naproxen 500 mg twice daily with partial relief and lisinopril 10 mg daily for hypertension. She denies fever, eye redness, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and mouth ulcers.

Vital signs, blood pressure 146/88, heart rate 78, weight 172 pounds. On exam the right second and third proximal interphalangeal joints are swollen and tender, with dactylitis of the right third finger. Total of six tender and three swollen joints. There are scaly plaques on both elbows and the scalp covering about three percent of body surface area, and mild nail pitting. No uveitis, no knee effusion.

Labs today: CRP 2.4 mg/dL, elevated, ESR 34, ALT 26, creatinine 0.8, hemoglobin 12.9, white blood cell count 6.2. Hand x-rays show mild joint space narrowing at the right third proximal interphalangeal joint without erosions.

Assessment, psoriatic arthritis with an active flare, driven mainly by missed adalimumab doses because of cost. Blood pressure is elevated, likely aggravated by naproxen.

Plan, increase methotrexate to 20 mg once weekly and continue folic acid 1 mg daily. Stop naproxen because of the blood pressure; continue lisinopril 10 mg daily and have primary care recheck her blood pressure in two weeks. Refer to our social worker and pharmacy team to apply for the manufacturer copay assistance program, and restart adalimumab 40 mg every other week once it is approved. If assistance is denied, we will discuss a lower-cost biosimilar. Repeat CRP, CBC, and ALT in four weeks for methotrexate monitoring. Follow up in six weeks.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
This is a dictation for a pulmonology follow-up visit on an 81-year-old female with obstructive sleep apnea on CPAP. She was diagnosed 16 months ago, correction, 14 months ago, with an AHI of 32 on her diagnostic study and has used an auto CPAP with a pressure range of 6 to 14 centimeters of water ever since. History of present illness, her main complaint today is that she does not like the mask. She says the air leaks around her full face mask, she has dry mouth, and she wakes up bloated from swallowing air so she often takes the mask off in the middle of the night. She still feels sleepy in the afternoon. She denies morning headaches, denies choking or gasping at night, denies falling asleep while talking or eating, and denies chest pain. Her Epworth score today is 11. Past history includes hypertension and hypothyroidism. Medications are amlodipine 5 mg daily, levothyroxine 50 mcg daily, and zolpidem 5 mg at bedtime, which her primary doctor started for insomnia 6 months ago. No known drug allergies. The CPAP download for the last 30 days shows use on 21 of 30 nights, average use 3.8 hours per night, use longer than 4 hours on only 38 percent of nights, a residual AHI of 4.1, and a 95th percentile leak of 38 liters per minute, which is high. Vitals today are blood pressure 136/78, pulse 70, oxygen saturation 96% on room air, BMI 31, and neck circumference 16 inches. On exam she is comfortable, Mallampati class 3, and lungs are clear. There is no leg edema. She has mild nasal congestion with pale turbinates. Assessment and plan, obstructive sleep apnea with suboptimal CPAP adherence because of mask leak, dry mouth, and aerophagia, and her residual events are low when she does wear it. Plan one, mask refit through her DME supplier with a different size full face mask and a chin strap. Plan two, increase the heated humidifier setting from 2 to 4. Plan three, change the auto CPAP range to 6 to 12 centimeters of water to reduce air swallowing. Plan four, start fluticasone nasal spray 50 mcg, one spray in each nostril once daily for the congestion. Plan five, stop zolpidem 5 mg because it can worsen sleep apnea and raises her fall risk at her age, and I will notify her primary doctor and recommend cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia. Repeat CPAP download in 6 weeks and return to clinic in 3 months. End of dictation.
"""

Nurse: Chart note for the doctor. This is a 63-year-old female here for a three-month follow-up after a pulmonary embolism. She has hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and osteoarthritis of the knees. Doctor: Good morning. It is nice to see you. Last time we talked about the blood clot in your lung. How have you been feeling?

Patient: Better, doctor. I still get a little tired and short of breath when I go up the stairs, but not like before.

Doctor: That can take a while to clear up. Any chest pain, or swelling in your legs?

Patient: No chest pain. No swelling in my legs either.

Doctor: Good. Have you coughed up any blood, or had nosebleeds, bleeding gums, or black stool?

Patient: No, none of that. I get a few bruises on my arms, but they go away.

Doctor: Okay. I want to make sure we get your medicines right. Tell me how you take your blood thinner, the apixaban.

Patient: The pink pill? I take one in the morning, with my breakfast.

Doctor: Just in the morning? Can you read me what the bottle says?

Patient: Let me see. It says five milligrams, take one tablet two times a day. Oh. Two times. I take one in the morning and one at night, yes. My daughter put them in the pill box with two rows. I said it wrong, sorry.

Doctor: That is fine, thank you for checking. So the right way is apixaban 5 mg, one pill morning and one pill night. Can you tell me that back in your own words?

Patient: One pink pill in the morning and one at night, every day. And I do not stop it unless you say.

Doctor: Perfect. What other medicines do you take?

Patient: Lisinopril 10 mg, the one for pressure, once a day. Metformin 500 mg twice a day for the sugar. Atorvastatin 20 mg at night. For my knees I take acetaminophen when needed, 500 mg. And a ginkgo pill from the store for my memory.

Doctor: Thank you. The ginkgo can make you bleed more with the blood thinner, so I would like you to stop it. Do you take any ibuprofen, naproxen, or other anti-inflammatory pain pills?

Patient: No. They gave me hives, so I never take them.

Doctor: Good, please keep avoiding them, because they are also risky with a blood thinner. Now, your blood tests today. Hemoglobin is 13.0, platelets are 250, and creatinine is 0.9, so your kidneys are handling the medicine well. The echocardiogram you had last month showed the right side of your heart is a normal size and the pressure in your lungs is normal. Your blood pressure today is a little high for someone with diabetes, 134 over 80. I would like it under 130 over 80.

Patient: So what do I change?

Doctor: Here is the plan. Number one, keep taking apixaban 5 mg twice a day. At six months we will talk about whether to lower it. Number two, increase your lisinopril from 10 mg to 20 mg once a day. Number three, stop the ginkgo. Number four, keep the acetaminophen for your knees, but no more than six of the 500 mg pills in one day. Can you tell me what you will change?

Patient: Stop the ginkgo. And take two of my lisinopril pills, the 10 mg ones I have at home, in the morning?

Doctor: Yes, exactly, two of the 10 mg pills once a day makes 20 mg. We will check a basic metabolic panel in two weeks to make sure the lisinopril is agreeing with your kidneys. Call us if you see black stool, blood in your urine, or a nosebleed that lasts more than ten minutes. Call 911 for sudden chest pain or trouble breathing. I will see you again in three months.

Patient: Okay, I understand. Thank you.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: Welcome back. This is your six-week postpartum visit after your cesarean, and I have you down as a 41-year-old female. How are you doing?
Patient: Tired, honestly. I'm back at work and I do rotating night and day shifts at a laundry, so my sleep is all over the place, and the baby is up every three hours.
Doctor: That sounds exhausting. How is your mood? Any days where you feel really down or hopeless?
Patient: Some tearful days, mostly when I haven't slept. But I don't feel hopeless, and I have not had any thoughts of hurting myself or the baby.
Doctor: I'm glad you told me. Your Edinburgh score on the form today was 8, which is below the cutoff, but we will recheck it. Any heavy bleeding?
Patient: No, the bleeding stopped about two weeks ago. No fever either.
Doctor: How is your incision? Any redness, drainage, or pain?
Patient: It's fine, no drainage. A little pulling when I lift the baby.
Doctor: Any chest pain, shortness of breath, or calf pain?
Patient: No, none of that.
Doctor: Are you breastfeeding?
Patient: Yes, and pumping at work when I can, but my break times change every week.
Doctor: Okay. You had high blood pressure at the end of the pregnancy and went home on labetalol 200 mg twice a day. How have your pressures been at home?
Patient: Around 115 over 70 for two weeks now. I've felt a bit lightheaded when I stand up. I also take ibuprofen 600 mg for the incision when it bothers me.
Doctor: Your blood pressure today is 112 over 70 with a heart rate of 74. With the lightheadedness, I want you to stop the labetalol now. Your incision is well healed without redness or drainage, your uterus is firm and not tender, and your breasts are normal. Your hemoglobin today was 9.6, up from 8.4 after delivery, so you are still anemic. I'm starting ferrous sulfate 325 mg once a day. Take it whenever you wake up, even if that is mid-afternoon, with some orange juice. The ibuprofen is fine to keep using as needed while you are breastfeeding.
Patient: What about birth control? A daily pill would be hard with my schedule.
Doctor: I agree. A levonorgestrel IUD would suit you well because there is nothing to remember. We can place it at a visit in two weeks, and until then please use condoms. I'll also repeat your CBC and ferritin in six weeks and recheck the Edinburgh form then. I'll write a note for your employer about pumping breaks.
Patient: Thank you, that would help a lot.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Gynecology clinic dictation. The patient is a 53-year-old female seen for abnormal uterine bleeding. She reports four months of irregular, heavy periods, with cycles coming every 2 to 3 weeks and bleeding lasting up to 10 days. On the heaviest days she soaks a pad every 1 to 2 hours and passes clots the size of a quarter. She also feels tired and lightheaded when she stands up. She denies pelvic pain, bleeding after intercourse, vaginal discharge, fever, weight loss, and chest pain. She has not yet gone 12 months without a period.

Past history includes hypothyroidism, on levothyroxine 75 mcg daily with a normal TSH of 2.1 last month, and two vaginal deliveries. No history of blood clots and no known bleeding disorder. She takes no hormonal medications. For cramps during the bleeding she takes ibuprofen 600 mg every 6 hours as needed. No known drug allergies. Her last Pap smear and HPV co-test two years ago were normal.

Vital signs: blood pressure 112/70, heart rate 92, temperature 98.2 F. On exam she looks pale with pale conjunctivae. Abdomen is soft, nontender, with no masses. Speculum exam shows moderate blood in the vaginal vault, a normal appearing cervix without lesions, and a closed os. Bimanual exam shows a uterus about 10 weeks in size, mobile, nontender, with an irregular contour, and no adnexal masses or tenderness.

Data. Urine pregnancy test is negative. Hemoglobin is 9.8 and ferritin is 8. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an endometrial thickness of 12 mm and a 3 cm intramural fibroid in the anterior wall, with normal ovaries. An endometrial biopsy was obtained today with a Pipelle catheter, the sample was adequate, she tolerated it well, and it was sent to pathology.

Assessment. One, abnormal uterine bleeding in the perimenopausal period, likely related to the fibroid and anovulation, with endometrial hyperplasia not yet excluded pending the biopsy. Two, iron deficiency anemia from the blood loss. Three, hypothyroidism, well controlled.

Plan. Start ferrous sulfate 325 mg once daily. Start tranexamic acid 1300 mg three times daily for up to 5 days during heavy bleeding. Continue ibuprofen as needed with food, and continue levothyroxine. Await the biopsy result. If it is benign, we will discuss a levonorgestrel intrauterine system versus a hysteroscopic procedure for the fibroid. Repeat hemoglobin in 6 weeks. She will return in 2 weeks to review the pathology, and she should go to the emergency department if she soaks more than one pad an hour for 2 hours or becomes dizzy or faint.
"""

Hospital day 3 for a 79-year-old female with Parkinson disease who was admitted with a urinary tract infection and worsening gait freezing. No overnight events. Medication reconciliation with the pharmacist clarified what she takes at home. Her prescribed medicines are carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 mg one tablet three times daily and pramipexole 0.25 mg three times daily. She also buys over-the-counter supplements without telling her doctors: ferrous sulfate 325 mg once daily, which she takes together with her morning carbidopa-levodopa dose, and ginkgo biloba, which she takes for memory. Iron can reduce levodopa absorption, which may be contributing to her morning and afternoon off periods. She denies orthostatic lightheadedness.

Current inpatient medications are ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily, carbidopa-levodopa, and pramipexole as above.

Data: Urine culture grew E. coli sensitive to ceftriaxone. WBC 8.4, down from 12.1 on admission. Creatinine 0.9. Hemoglobin 11.8.

Impression: Parkinson disease with end-of-dose wearing off, likely worsened by iron taken with levodopa and by the acute infection. E. coli urinary tract infection, improving. Mild anemia, which is probably why she started the iron on her own.

Changes and recommendations today: Increase carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 mg to one tablet four times daily, with the doses spaced evenly through the day. Stop ferrous sulfate and ginkgo biloba for now; if iron is still needed after an outpatient anemia work-up, it should be taken at least 2 hours away from levodopa. Continue pramipexole 0.25 mg three times daily. Continue ceftriaxone today, then change to cephalexin 500 mg twice daily to complete 7 days of treatment. Physical therapy and occupational therapy to evaluate gait and fall risk. Anticipate discharge tomorrow with neurology follow-up in 4 weeks.
"""

Doctor: Good morning. I understand you're a 71-year-old male scheduled for a right knee replacement in three weeks, and your surgeon wants me to check your heart first. Is that right?
Patient: Yes, doc. My knee has been terrible for years, so I'm ready to get it done.
Doctor: Do you ever get chest pain or pressure, either at rest or when you're active?
Patient: No chest pain at all.
Doctor: Shortness of breath, palpitations, or fainting spells?
Patient: None of those.
Doctor: How active are you? Can you climb a couple of flights of stairs without stopping?
Patient: I can climb two flights, a little slow because of the knee, but I don't get winded. I also walk the dog a mile every morning.
Doctor: That's good functional capacity. Any history of heart attack, stroke, heart failure, diabetes, or kidney problems?
Patient: No, just high blood pressure.
Doctor: What do you take for it?
Patient: Amlodipine, 5 mg once a day.
Doctor: Any problems with anesthesia in the past?
Patient: I had a hernia repair years ago and it went fine.
Doctor: Good. Your blood pressure today is 128/76 and your heart rate is 70 and regular. Your heart sounds are normal with no murmur, your lungs are clear, and there's no swelling in your ankles. Your ECG shows normal sinus rhythm with no signs of an old heart attack or ischemia.
Doctor: So my impression is that you're at low risk for cardiac complications with this surgery. You have good functional capacity, no heart symptoms, and a normal ECG, so you don't need a stress test or an echocardiogram. Continue amlodipine 5 mg daily, including the morning of surgery with a sip of water. I'll send a note to your surgeon, and we don't need to see you again unless something changes.
Patient: That's a relief. Thank you.

Doctor: Tell me about those flare-ups.
Patient: The first one in November, my cough got worse and the phlegm turned yellow, and my primary doctor gave me steroids and an antibiotic. The second one was in February, same thing, same treatment. I wasn't in the hospital either time.
Doctor: Any fever, chest pain, leg swelling, or coughing up blood?
Patient: No fever. No chest pain. No swelling in my legs. And no blood when I cough.

Doctor: Do you still smoke?
Patient: I do, about ten cigarettes a day. I've smoked since I was eighteen. I know I should quit.
Doctor: I appreciate you being honest, and we'll talk about that. Let me go over your numbers. Blood pressure is 142/84, heart rate 88, and oxygen saturation 93% on room air. Your lungs show diminished breath sounds with a prolonged expiratory phase and no wheezes, and there is no leg edema. Your spirometry today shows an FEV1 of 52 percent of predicted and an FEV1 to FVC ratio of 0.58, so you have moderate to severe COPD. Keep the albuterol for rescue, and rinse your mouth after each use of the Trelegy.
Patient: Okay.
Doctor: For smoking, I recommend a nicotine patch, 14 mg every 24 hours, to start. Quitting is the single most important thing we can do to slow this down. I'm also ordering a low-dose CT scan of the chest for lung cancer screening, referring you to pulmonary rehab, and recommending a pneumococcal vaccine and a flu shot this fall. Let's see you again in three months.
Patient: I'll try the patch.
"""

"""
Dermatology follow-up on the ward, hospital day 3, for a 57-year-old male with moderate plaque psoriasis. He has been on secukinumab 300 mg subcutaneously every 4 weeks for about a year and had good control until two months ago, when the plaques on his elbows and knees began to thicken and scale again. He admits to heavy alcohol use, about a pint of whiskey daily, and says his skin flares during his heaviest drinking weeks. He denies joint pain, morning stiffness, and fever. He reports he has not missed any secukinumab injections.

Vitals this morning are temperature 98.4 F, heart rate 88, and blood pressure 132/84. On exam there are well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale over both elbows and both knees, covering roughly 6 percent of body surface area. There are no pustules and no nail pitting, and there is no sign of skin infection. The scalp is clear.

My impression is moderate plaque psoriasis, incompletely controlled on secukinumab and aggravated by heavy alcohol use. I will continue secukinumab 300 mg every 4 weeks and start betamethasone dipropionate 0.05% ointment twice daily to the plaques for 2 weeks. A hepatic function panel will be sent today. I counseled him to cut back on alcohol, and I asked social work to arrange substance use counseling before discharge. He should return to dermatology clinic in 6 weeks.
"""

"""
The patient is a 20-year-old male seen in the urology clinic for follow-up of a right kidney stone. Two weeks ago he was seen in the emergency department with right flank pain radiating to the groin, and a CT scan showed a 5 mm stone in the right distal ureter and a 4 mm non-obstructing stone in the left lower pole of the kidney. He was sent home on tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily and ibuprofen 400 mg every 6 hours as needed, with a urine strainer. He passed the stone 9 days ago after a day of severe pain and caught it in the strainer. Since then the right flank pain has resolved. He denies fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, visible blood in the urine, and burning with urination. He stopped the ibuprofen on his own after the stone passed and is still taking tamsulosin.

This is his first stone episode. He drinks about 3 cups of fluid a day, mostly coffee and soda, and eats a lot of salty processed food. About 4 months ago he started a vitamin C supplement 1000 mg daily and a daily protein shake for weight training. His father had kidney stones. He has no other medical conditions and takes no other medicines.

On exam today BP 122/74, HR 66, and temperature 98.2 F. He is well appearing. There is no costovertebral angle tenderness on either side, and the abdomen is soft and nontender.

Stone analysis of the passed stone returned calcium oxalate monohydrate. Urinalysis today shows 3 to 5 red blood cells per high power field, with no white cells and no nitrite. Creatinine is 0.9, and serum calcium and uric acid are within normal limits.

Impression: First episode of calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis with spontaneous passage of the right ureteral stone, plus a residual 4 mm non-obstructing left lower pole stone. Contributing factors are low fluid intake, high sodium intake from processed food, and a vitamin C supplement.

Recommendations: Stop tamsulosin now that the stone has passed, and stop the vitamin C supplement. Increase fluids to about 3 liters a day, cut back on salty processed food, keep normal dietary calcium, and moderate the protein shakes. Order a 24-hour urine collection for stone risk and a PTH level. Renal ultrasound in 6 months to follow the left stone. Ibuprofen only if needed for pain. Return sooner for fever, severe flank pain, or vomiting. Follow up in clinic in 3 months with the 24-hour urine results.
"""

Two weeks ago he was seen in the emergency department with right flank pain radiating to the groin, and a CT scan showed a 5 mm stone in the right distal ureter and a 4 mm non-obstructing stone in the left lower pole of the kidney. He was sent home on tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily and ibuprofen 400 mg every 6 hours as needed, with a urine strainer. He passed the stone 9 days ago after a day of severe pain and caught it in the strainer. Since then the right flank pain has resolved. He denies fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, visible blood in the urine, and burning with urination. He stopped the ibuprofen on his own after the stone passed and is still taking tamsulosin.

This is his first stone episode. He drinks about 3 cups of fluid a day, mostly coffee and soda, and eats a lot of salty processed food. About 4 months ago he started a vitamin C supplement 1000 mg daily and a daily protein shake for weight training. His father had kidney stones. He has no other medical conditions and takes no other medicines.

On exam today BP 122/74, HR 66, and temperature 98.2 F. He is well appearing. There is no costovertebral angle tenderness on either side, and the abdomen is soft and nontender.

Stone analysis of the passed stone returned calcium oxalate monohydrate. Urinalysis today shows 3 to 5 red blood cells per high power field, with no white cells and no nitrite. Creatinine is 0.9, and serum calcium and uric acid are within normal limits.

Impression: First episode of calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis with spontaneous passage of the right ureteral stone, plus a residual 4 mm non-obstructing left lower pole stone. Contributing factors are low fluid intake, high sodium intake from processed food, and a vitamin C supplement.

Recommendations: Stop tamsulosin now that the stone has passed, and stop the vitamin C supplement. Increase fluids to about 3 liters a day, cut back on salty processed food, keep normal dietary calcium, and moderate the protein shakes. Order a 24-hour urine collection for stone risk and a PTH level. Renal ultrasound in 6 months to follow the left stone. Ibuprofen only if needed for pain. Return sooner for fever, severe flank pain, or vomiting. Follow up in clinic in 3 months with the 24-hour urine results.

Summarize the following clinical encounter note for a busy clinician.
Requirements:
- Write 3 to 6 sentences of plain prose (maximum 120 words), in the third person.
- Cover the patient's age/sex and reason for the visit, the key history and findings, the assessment, and the plan.
- Use only information stated in the note. Do not use headings or bullet points.

Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: Thanks for coming in. I have you down as a 29-year-old female here to go over the MRI of your left knee. Before we start, I see an allergy in your chart. Can you tell me about that?
Patient: Yes, I'm allergic to ibuprofen. I break out in hives and my lips swell. It happened twice, so I avoid all of those anti-inflammatory pills now.
Doctor: Good, I'll flag that you're allergic to ibuprofen and we will avoid NSAIDs completely. Now tell me how you hurt the knee.
Patient: I was playing soccer about two weeks ago. I planted my foot to turn, felt a pop, and the knee swelled up right away. I couldn't keep playing.
Doctor: So the injury was two weeks ago?
Patient: Sorry, no, three weeks ago. It was the weekend before my sister's wedding, and that was three weeks back.
Doctor: Thank you for clarifying. How does it feel now?
Patient: It gives way when I pivot or go down stairs. The swelling comes and goes. The pain is about a four after walking and nothing at rest.
Doctor: Any locking or catching, where the knee gets stuck?
Patient: No locking. And no numbness or tingling in my foot, and no calf pain.
Doctor: Any fever or redness around the knee?
Patient: No fever and no redness.
Doctor: What medicines do you take?
Patient: Levothyroxine, I think 50 micrograms every morning. Wait, no, it's 75 micrograms, I have the bottle in my bag, yes, 75. Sertraline 50 mg daily for anxiety. An albuterol inhaler, two puffs when I need it for my asthma. Sumatriptan 50 mg as needed for migraines. Acetaminophen 500 mg a few times a day for the knee. The urgent care also gave me cyclobenzaprine 5 mg at bedtime, but it made me groggy so I stopped it a week ago.
Doctor: Okay. Your primary care doctor checked a TSH last week and it was 6.8, which is high, so your thyroid dose is too low. Your hemoglobin was 13.1. Today your blood pressure is 114/70, pulse 68, and your BMI is 24.
Patient: Can you check the knee?
Doctor: Yes. There is a small effusion. Range of motion is 0 to 120 degrees. The Lachman test is positive with a soft endpoint, the anterior drawer is positive, and the pivot shift is positive. The knee is stable to varus and valgus stress, McMurray is negative, and I see mild quadriceps atrophy. The foot is warm with a good pulse and normal sensation. The MRI shows a complete mid-substance ACL tear with a bone bruise on the lateral femoral condyle, and the menisci and collateral ligaments are intact.
Patient: So what does that mean?
Doctor: My impression is a complete ACL tear of the left knee with instability, and your hypothyroidism is under-replaced. Your asthma and anxiety sound stable. Here is the plan. I recommend ACL reconstruction with a hamstring graft in about four weeks, after prehab. You'll start physical therapy now to restore your motion and strength, and use a hinged knee brace and crutches as needed. I'm increasing your levothyroxine from 75 to 88 micrograms every morning, and we'll recheck the TSH in six weeks. Keep the cyclobenzaprine stopped. For pain now, acetaminophen 1000 mg every 8 hours as needed. After surgery, acetaminophen 1000 mg every 8 hours on a schedule, plus oxycodone 5 mg every 6 hours as needed for three days. No NSAIDs at all, including ketorolac or celecoxib, before or after surgery, and I'll tell the anesthesia team about your ibuprofen allergy and your asthma. You'll have a urine pregnancy test before surgery. Come back in two weeks.
Patient: Okay, that makes sense. Thank you.
"""

Telehealth video visit, patient at home with good audio and video, for a 76-year-old male with right hand numbness. History is patient-reported, with a limited visual exam over video.

He shakes the hand to relieve it. He also notes a weaker grip and has dropped a coffee cup twice. He denies neck pain, denies weakness of the whole arm, denies a recent injury, and denies numbness in the left hand.

History includes type 2 diabetes and hypertension. Current medications are metformin 500 mg twice daily, lisinopril 10 mg daily, and ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day that he has been taking over the counter for hand pain. Home readings: BP 136/80 with a home cuff, pulse 72, and fasting glucose 128 this morning.

Transportation: He no longer drives and lives about 45 minutes from the clinic. He relies on a neighbor or a senior shuttle that runs only a few days a week, which makes in-person visits hard.

Limited video exam: Alert, in no distress, speaking in full sentences. No visible swelling, redness, or deformity of the right wrist. No visible thenar atrophy. He can make a full fist and oppose the thumb to each fingertip. With guidance he did the Phalen maneuver for 30 seconds and reproduced tingling in the thumb, index, and middle fingers, and self-tapping over the carpal tunnel produced tingling as well. Sensation and strength could not be formally tested over video.

Impression: Right carpal tunnel syndrome, likely related in part to his type 2 diabetes, a clinical diagnosis from history and provocative maneuvers. Hypertension is stable on home readings. NSAID use is not ideal with lisinopril and his age.

Recommendations: Stop ibuprofen and use acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed. If symptoms persist after six weeks of splinting, a corticosteroid injection could be done at that same in-person visit. Continue metformin and lisinopril. Telehealth follow-up in six weeks. Return sooner for worsening weakness, constant numbness, or muscle wasting in the hand.

This 82-year-old male returns to the nephrology clinic for follow-up of nephrotic syndrome. A kidney biopsy two months ago showed membranous nephropathy, and his anti-PLA2R antibody was positive. Over the past three weeks he has noticed more swelling in both legs and foamy urine, and his weight at home is up about 2 kg. He denies shortness of breath, orthopnea, chest pain, gross hematuria, flank pain, and fever. He has not used any NSAIDs or herbal supplements. His past history includes hypertension and hyperlipidemia. Current medications are lisinopril 10 mg daily, furosemide 40 mg daily, and atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, and he reports taking them reliably.

Vitals today show blood pressure 148/84, heart rate 72, respiratory rate 16, oxygen saturation 96% on room air, and weight 84.6 kg, compared with 82.4 kg at the last visit. On exam he is comfortable and speaks in full sentences. Jugular venous pressure is not elevated, the lungs are clear, and the heart sounds are regular. There is 2+ pitting edema of both legs to the knees and no ascites.

Labs drawn this morning show creatinine 1.3, eGFR 52, potassium 4.6, serum albumin 2.4 g/dL, LDL 162, and a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio of 6.8 g/g, which is increased from 5.2 last visit.

Reason for consultation: Routine HIV follow-up and review of antiretroviral therapy in a patient with several comorbidities and difficulty attending visits. Requesting service: primary care.

History of present illness: This is a 68-year-old male with HIV infection, diagnosed about twelve years ago according to the referral, correction, about fourteen years ago according to the old records, who is seen in the infectious disease specialty clinic for routine follow-up. He has taken efavirenz, emtricitabine, and tenofovir disoproxil fumarate as a single tablet at bedtime since shortly after diagnosis. He reports taking it nearly every night and has missed only one or two doses in the past month, which fits the pharmacy refill record. He lives about 90 miles from the clinic and has no reliable transportation, so he has missed two of his last four visits and relies on a neighbor to drive him. He denies fever, night sweats, unintentional weight loss, cough, diarrhea, rash, dysuria, and numbness or tingling in his feet. He does report vivid dreams and mild dizziness at night after taking the efavirenz tablet.

Past medical history: hypertension, type 2 diabetes, stage 3a chronic kidney disease, hyperlipidemia, and osteopenia. He has never had an opportunistic infection.

Medications: Metformin 500 mg twice daily, lisinopril 10 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, and calcium carbonate 600 mg daily taken over the counter. He first reported atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, but the pharmacy fill history confirms atorvastatin 40 mg nightly. He has no known drug allergies.

Social history: Retired, lives alone, former smoker who quit 15 years ago, drinks no alcohol, and has no injection drug use.

Physical examination: Blood pressure 148/86, heart rate 78, temperature 98.4 F, weight 82 kg. He is well appearing and in no distress. No oral thrush, no cervical or axillary lymphadenopathy, and no rash. Heart sounds are regular without murmur. Lungs are clear. Abdomen is soft and nontender. No peripheral edema. Monofilament sensation is intact in both feet.

Data review: CD4 count 612 cells per cubic millimeter and HIV-1 RNA less than 20 copies per milliliter, and he has been virologically suppressed for more than five years. Creatinine 1.4 mg/dL with eGFR 52. Urine albumin to creatinine ratio 85 mg/g, up from 40 mg/g a year ago. Hemoglobin A1c 7.4 percent, LDL 96, AST and ALT normal, hemoglobin 13.8 g/dL. Hepatitis B surface antigen negative with positive surface antibody, hepatitis C antibody negative, and syphilis screen negative. A DEXA scan last year showed osteopenia of the hip.

symptoms.text: bilateral shoulder and hip girdle pain

note:
Rheumatology inpatient progress note, hospital day 3. The patient is a 75-year-old male admitted with severe bilateral shoulder and hip girdle pain and stiffness who is being followed for polymyalgia rheumatica. A professional Spanish interpreter was used for the entire visit, and the history below was confirmed through the interpreter.

Overnight there were no events and he slept better than on previous nights. This morning he reports that his shoulder and hip pain is much better, about 3 out of 10 compared with 9 out of 10 on admission, and morning stiffness now lasts about 20 minutes instead of several hours. He walked to the bathroom with the physical therapist for the first time since admission.

His symptoms began about five weeks ago, shortly after he returned from a three-week trip to Mexico to visit relatives. Through the interpreter he denies fever, night sweats, weight loss, headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, vision changes, cough, and diarrhea.

Medication history: At first he said he was taking naproxen 250 mg twice daily for the pain. After the interpreter clarified the label with him, the correct dose is naproxen 500 mg twice daily, taken over the counter for the last four weeks. His other home medications are metformin 1000 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, and omeprazole 20 mg daily. He has no known drug allergies.

Hospital medications: Prednisone was started at 20 mg daily on admission and was decreased to 15 mg daily today because of his brisk response. Naproxen was stopped on admission. Metformin was held on admission and was resumed today. Calcium carbonate 600 mg twice daily and vitamin D3 1000 units daily were started for bone protection. Because of his recent travel and the start of steroids, he is receiving ivermectin 200 mcg/kg once daily for two days as prophylaxis for Strongyloides while the serology is pending.

Vitals this morning are temperature 98.2 F, BP 138/82, HR 74, RR 16, and SpO2 97% on room air. He is comfortable. There is no temporal artery tenderness and the temporal pulses are palpable. Active shoulder abduction has improved to 120 degrees from 60 degrees on admission. There is no synovitis in the hands, wrists, or knees and no rash. Lungs are clear.

Data: ESR is 52 mm/hr today, down from 78 on admission, and CRP is 21 mg/L, down from 62. Hemoglobin is 11.2 g/dL and creatinine is 1.0 mg/dL. Fasting glucose was 212 mg/dL this morning. ANA, rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP, and CK were normal or negative. QuantiFERON and hepatitis B surface antigen are negative. Strongyloides IgG is pending. Chest X-ray is clear.

Impression: Polymyalgia rheumatica with a brisk response to prednisone and no features of giant cell arteritis. Infectious and rheumatologic screens are negative so far. Steroid-associated hyperglycemia in the setting of type 2 diabetes mellitus. He also has hypertension and gastroesophageal reflux disease.

Plan: Continue prednisone 15 mg daily and taper slowly at outpatient rheumatology follow-up in two weeks. Finish ivermectin and follow up the Strongyloides IgG. Continue calcium and vitamin D3 and obtain an outpatient DEXA scan. Check fingerstick glucose before meals and at bedtime and add correction insulin as needed. Avoid NSAIDs from now on. Continue lisinopril, atorvastatin, and omeprazole. Review giant cell arteritis warning signs with him through the interpreter before discharge. Anticipate discharge tomorrow.

Telephone visit, audio only. The patient was at home and gave verbal consent to a telehealth visit. No video was available, so no physical examination could be performed.

Reason for visit: follow-up of left leg pain in a 70-year-old female with lumbar radiculopathy.

History per patient: She reports five weeks of low back pain with burning pain that travels down the left buttock, the outer thigh, and the calf to the top of the foot. The pain is 7 out of 10 at its worst, is worse with sitting and with coughing, and is a little better when she walks. She also has numbness and tingling over the top of the left foot. She denies bowel or bladder incontinence, saddle numbness, fever, progressive leg weakness, and recent falls. She says she can walk around her house and stand up from a chair without help.

Her other problems are hypertension and GERD. Medications she reports taking are amlodipine 5 mg once daily, omeprazole 20 mg once daily, ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily, which she has used for three weeks with little relief and which upsets her stomach, and acetaminophen 650 mg every six hours as needed.

Home readings today were blood pressure 138/80 and pulse 72 on her own cuff.

Data: An MRI of the lumbar spine two weeks ago, with the report read to the patient, shows a left paracentral disc extrusion at L4-L5 compressing the traversing left L5 nerve root, with moderate foraminal narrowing.

Impression: Left L5 lumbar radiculopathy due to an L4-L5 disc extrusion, with no red flag symptoms reported. Hypertension is stable by home readings, and GERD is stable on omeprazole.

Recommendations: Stop ibuprofen because of her stomach upset and blood pressure. Continue acetaminophen 650 mg every six hours as needed, not to exceed 3 grams per day. Start gabapentin 100 mg at bedtime, then increase to 100 mg three times daily after three days if she tolerates it, with counseling about drowsiness, dizziness, and fall precautions. Refer to physical therapy for core stabilization and nerve glide exercises. Encourage short walks and avoid prolonged bed rest. If the pain is not improved in four weeks, we will discuss an epidural steroid injection. She was told to go to the emergency department right away for new bowel or bladder incontinence, numbness in the saddle area, or worsening leg weakness. Follow-up telephone visit in four weeks.
"""

Patient: Not one.

Call right away if you get a fever, bloody stools, or can't keep fluids down.
Patient: Understood.
"""

"""
Doctor: Hello, thanks for coming in. I see you are a 34-year-old female here to talk about birth control. What are you looking for?
Patient: I have two kids and I am done for now, but I do not want anything permanent. I am using condoms and they are not great.
Doctor: Okay. Do you have any health problems or take any medicines?
Patient: I get migraines with aura, and I take sumatriptan 50 mg when one starts. And my periods are heavy.
Doctor: Any allergies to medicines?
Patient: Yes, ibuprofen gives me hives, so I cannot take ibuprofen or Advil or anything like it.
Doctor: Good to know, I will make sure nothing like that is prescribed. Do you smoke? Any chest pain, leg swelling, or pelvic pain?
Patient: I do not smoke. No chest pain, no leg swelling, and no pelvic pain. No bleeding between periods either.
Doctor: What about unusual discharge or pain with sex?
Patient: No discharge and no pain with sex.
Doctor: Thank you. Your blood pressure today is 112/70. Your urine pregnancy test is negative, and your Pap smear from last year was normal. On the exam, your abdomen is soft, and the uterus is normal in size, mobile, and not tender.
Patient: So what are my options?
Doctor: Because you have migraines with aura, you should not use any method that contains estrogen, so the pill, patch, and ring are out. A hormonal or a copper IUD would both work well for you. The levonorgestrel IUD would also make your heavy periods lighter, so I recommend that one. It lasts for years and is easy to remove if you change your mind.
Patient: Does it hurt to put in?
Doctor: Most people have cramping for a few minutes. Since you cannot take ibuprofen, I will have you take acetaminophen 1000 mg one hour before the insertion. Until the IUD is in, I would like you to start norethindrone 0.35 mg, one pill every day at the same time, as a bridge. It does not contain estrogen, so it is safe with your migraines. Keep using condoms for the first week.
Patient: Okay, that works for me.
Doctor: Keep the sumatriptan for your migraines as you have been. We will schedule the IUD insertion in two weeks, and I will see you for a check four to six weeks after that. Call us if you have heavy bleeding, fever, or severe belly pain after the insertion.
Patient: Thank you, Doctor.
"""

Patient: I have two kids and I am done for now, but I do not want anything permanent. I am using condoms and they are not great.
Doctor: Okay. Do you have any health problems or take any medicines?
Patient: I get migraines with aura, and I take sumatriptan 50 mg when one starts. And my periods are heavy.
Doctor: Any allergies to medicines?
Patient: Yes, ibuprofen gives me hives, so I cannot take ibuprofen or Advil or anything like it.
Doctor: Good to know, I will make sure nothing like that is prescribed. Do you smoke? Any chest pain, leg swelling, or pelvic pain?
Patient: I do not smoke. No chest pain, no leg swelling, and no pelvic pain. No bleeding between periods either.
Doctor: What about unusual discharge or pain with sex?
Patient: No discharge and no pain with sex.
Doctor: Thank you. Your blood pressure today is 112/70. Your urine pregnancy test is negative, and your Pap smear from last year was normal. On the exam, your abdomen is soft, and the uterus is normal in size, mobile, and not tender.
Patient: So what are my options?
Doctor: Because you have migraines with aura, you should not use any method that contains estrogen, so the pill, patch, and ring are out. A hormonal or a copper IUD would both work well for you. The levonorgestrel IUD would also make your heavy periods lighter, so I recommend that one. It lasts for years and is easy to remove if you change your mind.
Patient: Does it hurt to put in?
Doctor: Most people have cramping for a few minutes. Since you cannot take ibuprofen, I will have you take acetaminophen 1000 mg one hour before the insertion. Until the IUD is in, I would like you to start norethindrone 0.35 mg, one pill every day at the same time, as a bridge. It does not contain estrogen, so it is safe with your migraines. Keep using condoms for the first week.
Patient: Okay, that works for me.
Doctor: Keep the sumatriptan for your migraines as you have been. We will schedule the IUD insertion in two weeks, and I will see you for a check four to six weeks after that. Call us if you have heavy bleeding, fever, or severe belly pain after the insertion.
Patient: Thank you, Doctor.

Clinical note:
"""
Dermatology clinic dictation. This is a 37-year-old female seen for a changing mole on the upper back. She says it has grown larger and darker over the last 6 months and itches now and then. She denies bleeding, ulceration, or pain, and she has never had skin cancer. She had several blistering sunburns as a teenager and her mother had melanoma. She lives about 2 hours from the clinic, relies on a bus, and has missed visits before because of transportation. On exam there is a 9 mm brown to black macule on the right upper back, correction, the left upper back, with an irregular border and uneven color. On dermoscopy there is an atypical network with irregular blotches. There is no palpable lymphadenopathy in the neck or axillae and no other suspicious lesions on the full skin exam. Impression is an atypical pigmented lesion, rule out melanoma. Because of her transportation barrier we did an excisional biopsy with 2 mm margins today instead of scheduling a second trip. The site was numbed with 1% lidocaine with epinephrine, 3 mL, and closed with 4-0 nylon sutures, and the specimen went to dermatopathology. Wound care is petrolatum daily with a bandage. She will get the pathology result by video visit in about 1 week, and the sutures come out in 2 weeks at a clinic near her home, with a wider excision if melanoma is confirmed. End dictation.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Telehealth video visit, gastroenterology, conducted on a secure video platform with a professional Spanish interpreter on the call for the entire visit. The patient is a 54-year-old female referred by her primary care clinician to discuss colorectal cancer screening. She is at home in a quiet room.

She has never had a colonoscopy or any stool-based screening test. She appeared anxious and asked many questions, including how painful the preparation is, whether the sedation is safe, what could go wrong, what happens if a polyp is found, how much it costs, and whether a stool test is just as good. Each question was answered through the interpreter. She is worried because a relative had colon cancer; she first said her sister had it at age 60, then clarified that it was her maternal aunt, and that she has no first-degree relatives with colorectal cancer.

She denies rectal bleeding, black stools, abdominal pain, unintentional weight loss, and any change in bowel habits. She reports occasional mild constipation that responds to fluids.

Past history includes type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hypothyroidism, GERD, and hyperlipidemia. Current medications by her report are metformin 500 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, levothyroxine 100 mcg daily, omeprazole 20 mg daily, and atorvastatin 20 mg nightly. On reviewing the bottles by video she corrected the metformin: it is metformin ER 1000 mg once daily, not 500 mg twice daily. She has also been taking over-the-counter naproxen 220 mg for knee pain, about three times a week, and has had more heartburn recently. She takes no blood thinners. She has no known drug allergies.

Home readings this morning were blood pressure 130/82, heart rate 74, and fingerstick glucose 118, and her home scale weight was 78 kg. Results she had on hand from her primary care clinic show hemoglobin A1c 7.4%, LDL 142 mg/dL, and hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL two months ago.

On video she looked anxious but in no distress. She spoke in full sentences, had no visible jaundice or pallor, and moved comfortably. She pressed on her abdomen herself and reported no tenderness. A hands-on abdominal exam could not be done by video.

Impression is that she is at average risk for colorectal cancer with no alarm symptoms. I reviewed three options: colonoscopy every 10 years if normal, which also allows polyps to be removed during the same procedure; annual FIT; or a multi-target stool DNA test every 3 years. I explained that any positive stool test would still need a colonoscopy. After a long discussion she chose colonoscopy.

Plan is to schedule a screening colonoscopy in 4 to 6 weeks with sedation by an anesthesia team. She will use a split-dose polyethylene glycol bowel preparation, with written instructions in Spanish and teach-back through the interpreter. For her diabetes she should hold the metformin the morning of the procedure and check her glucose while on clear liquids. A nurse will call before the procedure to answer questions. Naproxen is stopped now because of the heartburn and the bleeding risk with polyp removal, and she can use acetaminophen 500 mg as needed for knee pain instead. Omeprazole is increased from 20 mg to 40 mg daily for 8 weeks. Her other medications continue unchanged. She needs an adult to drive her home after the procedure. She should call for heavy bleeding from the rectum, tarry stools, or severe belly pain.
"""

She denies rectal bleeding, black stools, abdominal pain, unintentional weight loss and change in bowel habits, and she has more heartburn from over-the-counter naproxen. The impression is average risk for colorectal cancer with no alarm symptoms, and after reviewing colonoscopy, FIT and stool DNA testing she chose colonoscopy. Naproxen is stopped, omeprazole is increased to 40 mg daily, and a split-dose bowel preparation with diabetes instructions was planned.

54-year-old female referred to discuss colorectal cancer screening, seen by video with a professional Spanish interpreter; never screened, anxious, and asked many questions about preparation, sedation, risks, polyps, cost and stool tests. A relative had colon cancer: she first said her sister at age 60, then clarified it was her maternal aunt, with no first-degree relatives affected. Denies rectal bleeding, black stools, abdominal pain, unintentional weight loss and change in bowel habits; occasional mild constipation. PMH type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hypothyroidism, GERD, hyperlipidemia. Medications: metformin ER 1000 mg once daily (first stated 500 mg twice daily, corrected after reviewing the bottle), lisinopril 20 mg daily, levothyroxine 100 mcg daily, omeprazole 20 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, and over-the-counter naproxen 220 mg about three times a week for knee pain with more heartburn recently. No blood thinners and no known drug allergies.

OBJECTIVE:
Home blood pressure 130/82, heart rate 74, fingerstick glucose 118, weight 78 kg. Recent primary care results: hemoglobin A1c 7.4%, LDL 142 mg/dL, hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL two months ago. Video exam: looked anxious but in no distress, spoke in full sentences, no visible jaundice or pallor, moved comfortably; self-palpation of the abdomen without tenderness; hands-on abdominal exam not possible by video.

ASSESSMENT:
Average risk for colorectal cancer with no alarm symptoms. Chronic conditions include type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hypothyroidism, GERD and hyperlipidemia, with heartburn aggravated by naproxen.

PLAN:
1. Reviewed colonoscopy every 10 years, annual FIT, and multi-target stool DNA test every 3 years; positive stool tests would still need colonoscopy; she chose colonoscopy
2. Schedule screening colonoscopy in 4 to 6 weeks with sedation by an anesthesia team
3. Split-dose polyethylene glycol bowel preparation with written instructions in Spanish and teach-back through the interpreter
4. Hold metformin the morning of the procedure and check glucose while on clear liquids
5. Nurse to call before the procedure to answer questions
6. Stop naproxen because of heartburn and the bleeding risk with polyp removal; use acetaminophen 500 mg as needed for knee pain
7. Increase omeprazole from 20 mg to 40 mg daily for 8 weeks
8. Continue other medications unchanged
9. Arrange an adult to drive her home after the procedure
10. Call for heavy bleeding from the rectum, tarry stools, or severe belly pain
note:
Telehealth video visit, gastroenterology, conducted on a secure video platform with a professional Spanish interpreter on the call for the entire visit. The patient is a 54-year-old female referred by her primary care clinician to discuss colorectal cancer screening. She is at home in a quiet room.

She has never had a colonoscopy or any stool-based screening test. She appeared anxious and asked many questions, including how painful the preparation is, whether the sedation is safe, what could go wrong, what happens if a polyp is found, how much it costs, and whether a stool test is just as good. Each question was answered through the interpreter. She is worried because a relative had colon cancer; she first said her sister had it at age 60, then clarified that it was her maternal aunt, and that she has no first-degree relatives with colorectal cancer.

She denies rectal bleeding, black stools, abdominal pain, unintentional weight loss, and any change in bowel habits. She reports occasional mild constipation that responds to fluids.

Past history includes type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hypothyroidism, GERD, and hyperlipidemia. Current medications by her report are metformin 500 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, levothyroxine 100 mcg daily, omeprazole 20 mg daily, and atorvastatin 20 mg nightly. On reviewing the bottles by video she corrected the metformin: it is metformin ER 1000 mg once daily, not 500 mg twice daily. She has also been taking over-the-counter naproxen 220 mg for knee pain, about three times a week, and has had more heartburn recently. She takes no blood thinners. She has no known drug allergies.

Home readings this morning were blood pressure 130/82, heart rate 74, and fingerstick glucose 118, and her home scale weight was 78 kg. Results she had on hand from her primary care clinic show hemoglobin A1c 7.4%, LDL 142 mg/dL, and hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL two months ago.

On video she looked anxious but in no distress. She spoke in full sentences, had no visible jaundice or pallor, and moved comfortably. She pressed on her abdomen herself and reported no tenderness. A hands-on abdominal exam could not be done by video.

Impression is that she is at average risk for colorectal cancer with no alarm symptoms. I reviewed three options: colonoscopy every 10 years if normal, which also allows polyps to be removed during the same procedure; annual FIT; or a multi-target stool DNA test every 3 years. I explained that any positive stool test would still need a colonoscopy. After a long discussion she chose colonoscopy.

Plan is to schedule a screening colonoscopy in 4 to 6 weeks with sedation by an anesthesia team. She will use a split-dose polyethylene glycol bowel preparation, with written instructions in Spanish and teach-back through the interpreter. For her diabetes she should hold the metformin the morning of the procedure and check her glucose while on clear liquids. A nurse will call before the procedure to answer questions. Naproxen is stopped now because of the heartburn and the bleeding risk with polyp removal, and she can use acetaminophen 500 mg as needed for knee pain instead. Omeprazole is increased from 20 mg to 40 mg daily for 8 weeks. Her other medications continue unchanged. She needs an adult to drive her home after the procedure. She should call for heavy bleeding from the rectum, tarry stools, or severe belly pain.

Summarize the following clinical encounter note for a busy clinician.
Requirements:
- Write 3 to 6 sentences of plain prose (maximum 120 words), in the third person.
- Cover the patient's age/sex and reason for the visit, the key history and findings, the assessment, and the plan.

Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: Good to see you again. For the record, I'm seeing a 54-year-old male for his COPD maintenance follow-up. How have you been since the last visit?

Patient: Not great, honestly. I still get winded going up the stairs at work, and the cough in the morning hasn't gone away.

Doctor: Tell me about the cough. Is it dry, or are you bringing up phlegm?

Patient: A spoonful of white phlegm in the morning, that's about it. No blood.

Doctor: Any fever, chills, or night sweats?

Patient: No fever, no chills, no night sweats.

Doctor: Any chest pain, or swelling in your ankles?

Patient: No chest pain and my ankles are fine. I do get a little wheeze at night when I lie flat, though.

Doctor: Any flare-ups since we last met?

Patient: Two in the past year. Both times I went to urgent care and they gave me steroids and an antibiotic. The second one was about two months ago.

Doctor: Which maintenance inhaler are you using, and how often?

Patient: The Anoro Ellipta, one puff every morning. I almost never miss it.

Doctor: And your rescue inhaler?

Patient: Albuterol, two puffs when I need it. I'd say once or twice a day.

Doctor: What else are you taking, including anything over the counter?

Patient: Lisinopril 10 mg once a day for hypertension, omeprazole 20 mg once a day for reflux, and atorvastatin 20 mg at night for high cholesterol. Over the counter I take fish oil, vitamin D, and a herbal lung support capsule from the health food store.

Doctor: How much vitamin D do you take?

Patient: 5,000 units a day. Hold on, let me check the bottle photo on my phone. No, it's 2,000 units daily. The 5,000 one was what I took last winter.

Doctor: Good, thank you for checking. What is in the herbal lung support capsule?

Patient: It lists mullein, ginseng, and licorice root. I take two capsules a day.

Doctor: Okay. Licorice root can raise blood pressure and lower potassium, so I would like you to stop that one. Do you still smoke?

Patient: No, I quit two years ago. I smoked about thirty pack-years.

Doctor: Good for you. Now your results. Vitals today: blood pressure 138/84, heart rate 82, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 94% on room air. On exam you have a prolonged expiratory phase and scattered expiratory wheezes, no crackles, and no leg edema. Your spirometry today shows a post-bronchodilator FEV1 of 52% of predicted and an FEV1 to FVC ratio of 0.58, about the same as last year. Your blood eosinophil count last week was 320, and the chest X-ray last month showed hyperinflation without any pneumonia.

Patient: So what does that mean?

Doctor: It means your COPD is moderate to severe, and with two flare-ups in a year despite dual therapy, plus the high eosinophils, you will benefit from a stronger inhaler. Your reflux can also make the cough worse, so we will increase the omeprazole.

Patient: Will the new inhaler interact with anything?

Doctor: No, not with your current medicines. Here is the plan. Stop the Anoro Ellipta and start Trelegy Ellipta, one inhalation once daily, and rinse your mouth afterward. Continue albuterol as needed. Increase omeprazole from 20 mg to 40 mg once daily. Stop the licorice herbal capsule, and you can continue the fish oil and the vitamin D at 2,000 units daily. I am referring you to pulmonary rehabilitation, ordering a yearly low-dose CT scan of the chest for lung cancer screening, and giving you a flu shot today. We will repeat spirometry in three months.

Patient: And if I get another flare-up?

Doctor: Call us the same day instead of waiting for urgent care. I will see you back in three months.
"""

reference: A 54-year-old male with COPD, hypertension, reflux and high cholesterol attended pulmonology follow-up for breathlessness on stairs and a morning cough with white phlegm, with two flare-ups in the past year. Anoro Ellipta was changed to Trelegy Ellipta, omeprazole was increased to 40 mg, and the herbal capsule was stopped. Clinical note:
"""
This is a hospital ward progress dictation on a 32-year-old male with Crohn's disease, hospital day 3. He was admitted two days ago with a Crohn's disease flare. He is a recent readmission, because he was discharged from this hospital about three weeks ago after a flare that was treated with intravenous steroids. He has ileocolonic Crohn's disease diagnosed years ago and takes adalimumab 40 mg every other week. He has a documented sulfa allergy, which caused a diffuse rash, so sulfasalazine is not an option for him.

At home he was finishing a prednisone taper from the last admission. He first told me he was taking prednisone 10 mg daily when the symptoms came back, correction, he brought the bottle in and he was actually taking 20 mg daily and had not tapered below that. He was also using loperamide as needed for the diarrhea and ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily.

Interval history, he reports eight to ten loose watery stools a day including nighttime stools, with crampy right lower quadrant abdominal pain and about six pounds of weight loss over the last month. Overnight he had five stools and some nausea. He denies fever, vomiting, blood in the stool, perianal pain and mouth sores.

Current inpatient medications are methylprednisolone 30 mg IV every 12 hours, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously daily for VTE prophylaxis, ondansetron 4 mg IV every 8 hours as needed for nausea, and lactated Ringer's at 100 mL per hour. Potassium chloride 40 mEq by mouth was given yesterday for repletion.

Vitals this morning, temperature 99.1, heart rate 96, blood pressure 112 over 68, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air.

On exam he is thin but in no distress. Abdomen is soft with mild tenderness in the right lower quadrant, no rebound, no guarding, and no distension. Bowel sounds are present. Perianal exam shows no fistula or abscess, and there are no oral ulcers.

Data, hemoglobin 10.1, WBC 11.8, platelets 480, CRP 78, albumin 3.0, potassium 3.4 on admission and 3.9 this morning, creatinine 0.8. Ferritin is low at 14. C. difficile PCR and stool culture were both negative. CT enterography on admission showed a 15 cm segment of terminal ileal wall thickening with mucosal hyperenhancement and no abscess or obstruction.

My impression is a moderate to severe Crohn's disease flare in a patient on adalimumab, with anemia, hypokalemia that has now been corrected, and low albumin.

As for management, one, the home prednisone is discontinued and he will stay on methylprednisolone 30 mg IV every 12 hours for now. Two, stop loperamide and avoid antimotility agents during the flare. Three, send an adalimumab trough level with antibodies, and given the flare on every other week dosing I will intensify adalimumab to 40 mg weekly starting with the next scheduled dose. Five, stop oral ferrous sulfate because it worsens his stomach upset, and give iron sucrose 200 mg IV for the iron deficiency. Six, dietitian consult for nutrition support. Seven, repeat CRP and BMP in the morning. He will not receive sulfasalazine because of the sulfa allergy. Expected discharge is in three to four days on a prednisone taper, with GI clinic follow-up within one week, and he understands to return for worsening pain, fever or bleeding.
"""

"""
60-year-old female, new pt, pulm clinic. Referred by PCP for chronic cough x 4 mo.
